newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: India urged to back reward for Kashmir hostages.
newsitem.headline: India urged to back reward for Kashmir hostages.

text.p: Britain, Germany and the United States have asked India to support a proposal to offer a small reward for information about four Westerners taken captive in Kashmir last year, the wife of the U.S. hostage said on Monday.

Jane Schelly, wife of hostage Donald Hutchings, told Reuters the governments whose nationals were kidnapped in July 1995 have thrown their support behind a U.S. proposal to offer a modest financial reward for information about the hostages.
The foreign governments were now awaiting a decision by the governments of India and the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir, where the tourists were kidnapped 16 months ago, she said.
"I personally would like to see a very small monetary incentive to motivate someone who might have information but who would be reluctant to come forth with it," Schelly told a news conference.
She was joined by the wife and parents of British hostage Keith Mangan. They travelled to Pakistan last week from India to seek information about their relatives.

Hutchings and Mangan were kidnapped with American John Childs and Briton Paul Wells on July 4, 1995, while trekking in Kashmir. Four days later, Childs escaped and German Dirk Hasert and Norwegian Hans Christian Ostroe were captured by the same Al-Faran guerrillas. Ostroe was beheaded in August.

Schelly, Mangan's wife Julie and his parents Mavis and Charles Mangan said that after three weeks of searching for information in the Kashmir valley, Pakistan-ruled Azad (Free) Kashmir, Delhi and Islamabad, they did not know if the hostages were dead or alive.

"Everywhere we have received sympathy," Mavis Mangan said, reading a statement by the hostages' relatives. "But nowhere have we received hard news. Someone, somewhere knows the truth. Please stop torturing us with your silence."
Schelly, who first raised the possibility of a financial reward, said Britain had initially been reluctant to support the proposal but was now backing it along with Germany.
Julie Mangan said the relatives of the other hostages had also been reluctant at first to press for a reward for fear it could be construed as ransom and prompt subsequent kidnappings.
"At first we were a little worried," Julie Mangan said, adding that the families did not want to encourage "copy cats".
"It has been very hard for us to come to a decision. We all got our heads together and we decided that we would be very much in favour of it," she said.

Schelly said she favoured "a very small monetary reward". Diplomats have said the reward, which could be offered under a U.S. programme providing for up to $2 million, might be for 100,000 Indian rupees ($2,775) or less.
She said the Western governments were awaiting a decision by New Delhi and the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir state, Farooq Abdullah.
The hostages' relatives said the Western governments had given a list of suspected kidnappers to Pakistan. Schelly said she had requested a meeting with Pakistani Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto.

India believes Al-Faran has links to Pakistan-based Harkat-ul-Ansar guerrillas. Pakistan denies Delhi's claims that Islamabad arms and trains militants fighting Indian rule in Jammu and Kashmir, where some 20,000 people have died in a seven-year separatist insurgency.
Schelly told Reuters she would return to the Kashmir valley to seek an explanation from Farooq Abdullah, who recently said he had received a report that the hostages had been sighted.
